pillars.name: Coachability
pillars.tagline: The ability to receive feedback, adapt, improve, and continuously learn.
pillars.definition: Coachability is the willingness to accept feedback, adjust behavior, and improve over time. Coachable leaders treat correction as information—not insult—and use it to get better on the next shift.
pillars.whyItMatters: On the production floor, standards change, equipment evolves, and safety expectations tighten. Leaders who learn quickly outperform those who rely on tenure alone. Coachability determines how fast someone closes the gap between where they are and where the operation needs them to be.
behaviors: Describes specific feedback received and how behavior changed afterward
Credits mentors, trainers, and prior leaders for their development
Shares concrete examples of skills improved within the last year
Owns mistakes on safety, quality, or production without deflecting
Asks questions, seeks clarification, and applies new SOPs without resistance
warningSigns: Blames equipment, coworkers, or management when results fall short
Cannot recall a time they were corrected or coached
Becomes defensive when discussing gaps in performance
Imply they already know what the team needs
Interview answers focus on credentials rather than growth
interviewQuestions: Tell me about a time you received difficult feedback on the job. What did you do next?
What skill have you deliberately improved in the past twelve months?
Describe a situation where you realized your approach was wrong.
Tell me about an early-career struggle and how you worked through it.
coachingTips: Deliver direct feedback after gemba walks and observe whether behavior changes on the next shift.
Assign a stretch task slightly beyond current skill—then debrief what was learned.
Use a simple format after mistakes: what happened, what you own, what changes tomorrow.
Pair with a strong shift lead for 30 days and track openness to guidance.
Recognize leaders who ask for feedback before problems escalate.

evaluationScale.label: Resistant
evaluationScale.description: Rejects feedback, repeats errors, and discourages coaching on the floor.

evaluationScale.label: Reluctant
evaluationScale.description: Agrees in conversation but rarely changes behavior on shift.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Applies feedback with prompting; improvement is visible but inconsistent.

evaluationScale.label: Responsive
evaluationScale.description: Adjusts quickly and shows measurable improvement without repeated reminders.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Seeks feedback proactively and accelerates learning across the team.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Coachability predicts how quickly a leader will grow once the title changes—often more reliably than years of experience.

pillars.name: Discipline
pillars.tagline: The ability to consistently execute the right actions regardless of motivation, circumstances, or obstacles.
pillars.definition: Discipline is doing what the operation requires—every shift—not only when conditions are ideal. It shows up in routines, follow-through, and adherence to standards when no one is watching.
pillars.whyItMatters: Plants run on consistency. Disciplined leaders maintain 5S, complete audits, hold huddles, and close action items whether production is smooth or under pressure. Without discipline, talent produces spikes—not sustained operational excellence.
behaviors: Follows through on commitments without reminders
Maintains personal routines that support shift readiness and team standards
Can explain the systems and checklists they rely on daily
Prepares before critical events: launches, audits, staffing gaps, or customer visits
Holds self and team to safety, quality, and production standards equally
warningSigns: Starts initiatives but rarely finishes them
Attributes missed targets to motivation rather than execution
Cannot describe consistent habits that support performance
Talks about what they intend to do more than what they actually do
Struggles to cite examples of sustained effort over months
interviewQuestions: Tell me about a long-term goal that required sustained effort on the floor.
What routine or process helps you perform consistently shift after shift?
What do you do reliably that others on your team often skip?
Describe a period when results were slow—how did you stay committed?
coachingTips: Establish non-negotiable daily rhythms: pre-shift review, gemba, end-of-shift handoff.
Track standards visibly—SQDC boards, audit scores, and action-item closure rates.
Coach with checklists and cadence, not motivation speeches.
Address inconsistency early; lax standards spread faster than good ones.
Model the discipline you expect—your team mirrors your follow-through.

evaluationScale.label: Inconsistent
evaluationScale.description: Execution depends on mood or external pressure; standards slip routinely.

evaluationScale.label: Sporadic
evaluationScale.description: Performs well in bursts but cannot sustain fundamentals over time.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Meets standards with reminders; improving but not yet self-directed.

evaluationScale.label: Reliable
evaluationScale.description: Executes core routines without supervision across varying conditions.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Builds team-wide systems that make disciplined execution the default.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Discipline converts potential into predictable results—the foundation every other pillar depends on.

pillars.name: Accountability
pillars.tagline: The willingness to take ownership of actions, decisions, results, and outcomes without blaming others.
pillars.definition: Accountability means owning outcomes—good and bad. Accountable leaders answer for shift results, close loops on issues, and drive solutions instead of explanations.
pillars.whyItMatters: When scrap rises, downtime hits, or a safety near-miss occurs, the organization needs leaders who step forward—not sideways. Accountability builds trust, shortens problem-solving cycles, and keeps continuous improvement from stalling in blame.
behaviors: Names their role in failures and describes corrective action taken
Focuses conversations on solutions, containment, and prevention
Learns openly from missed targets and quality escapes
Accepts responsibility for team performance—not only individual tasks
Closes commitments on time: CAPA items, audits, training, and escalations
warningSigns: Defaults to blaming maintenance, planning, or prior shift
Unable to identify a personal mistake in the last year
Discusses problems without owning a path forward
Excuses persist even when patterns repeat
Emphasizes what others failed to do rather than what they control
interviewQuestions: Tell me about a significant mistake you made and what you learned.
Describe a time you missed a production or quality target.
How do you respond when your team underperforms on shift?
Tell me about a problem you inherited—how did you take ownership?
coachingTips: Separate blame from ownership: focus on facts, impact, and next actions.
Run brief after-action reviews after major incidents or customer issues.
Track whether leaders close their own action items before chasing the team's.
Reward transparent ownership—even when the news is bad.
Address deflection patterns immediately; they erode shift culture fast.

evaluationScale.label: Deflecting
evaluationScale.description: Consistently shifts responsibility; team learns to hide problems.

evaluationScale.label: Selective
evaluationScale.description: Owns wins but distances from failures or team breakdowns.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Takes ownership when prompted; follow-through is improving.

evaluationScale.label: Accountable
evaluationScale.description: Owns results proactively and drives solutions without excuses.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Models ownership under pressure and builds a team that does the same.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Teams trust leaders who tell the truth about results and fix problems—not leaders who protect ego.

pillars.name: Competitive Drive
pillars.tagline: The internal desire to improve, win, raise standards, and pursue better results.
pillars.definition: Competitive drive is the hunger to improve—against last week's numbers, last year's benchmark, and the standard the operation truly requires. It is not ego. It is caring deeply about results.
pillars.whyItMatters: Average plants accept average. Leaders with competitive drive push OEE, reduce waste, raise quality, and energize teams around shared targets. They notice drift before it becomes normal.
behaviors: Talks about metrics, trends, and improvement with specificity
Sets goals for self and team beyond minimum expectations
Celebrates progress while raising the bar
Identifies gaps quickly and mobilizes the team to close them
Shows pride in team results—not personal spotlight alone
warningSigns: Indifferent toward targets, rankings, or plant performance
Accepts missed goals if explanations sound reasonable
Competes internally in ways that damage collaboration
Motivation appears tied only to recognition, not results
Cannot articulate what improvement looks like on their shift
interviewQuestions: Tell me about a goal you set that required you to push beyond comfort.
What does winning look like on a manufacturing floor?
Describe a process, metric, or result you improved.
What drives you when no one is watching?
coachingTips: Tie competitive energy to team KPIs: safety, quality, delivery, cost.
Review trend data weekly—not just end-of-month scorecards.
Correct toxic competitiveness early; standards beat politics.
Pair drive with humility and coachability for sustainable leadership.
Benchmark against prior periods and best-performing shifts, not excuses.

evaluationScale.label: Complacent
evaluationScale.description: Shows little interest in improving plant or team performance.

evaluationScale.label: Passive
evaluationScale.description: Responds when pushed but does not self-initiate improvement.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Engaged with results; needs structure to sustain momentum.

evaluationScale.label: Driven
evaluationScale.description: Consistently pursues improvement and lifts team expectations.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Inspires operational excellence; competes against standards, not people.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Drive moves teams forward—when it serves the shift, the plant, and the customer—not personal status.

pillars.name: Pressure Response
pillars.tagline: How a person behaves when expectations, stress, uncertainty, and consequences increase.
pillars.definition: Pressure response is composure and decision quality when the line stops, the customer calls, staffing is thin, or the schedule breaks. It is how a leader shows up when the cost of error is highest.
pillars.whyItMatters: Fair-weather leadership is common. Real leadership appears during breakdowns, quality holds, safety incidents, and end-of-quarter pushes. Plants need supervisors who think clearly when others react.
behaviors: Stays calm and directs attention to facts, safety, and containment
Communicates clearly during disruptions—who, what, when, next step
Prioritizes effectively when multiple issues compete for attention
Maintains standards under stress; does not shortcut procedures
Recovers team momentum after setbacks without blame spirals
warningSigns: Visible frustration, yelling, or panic during disruptions
Blames others while the line is still down
Avoids decisions when information is incomplete
Freezes or scatter-focuses when priorities shift suddenly
Team morale drops sharply during high-pressure periods
interviewQuestions: Tell me about the most stressful situation you faced in operations.
Describe a major problem that hit without warning—walk me through your response.
How do you prioritize when safety, quality, and production all demand attention?
Tell me about a decision you made with incomplete information.
coachingTips: Debrief real events: line stops, escapes, staffing crises—what worked, what to repeat.
Practice escalation paths and priority frameworks before emergencies.
Observe leaders during actual disruptions, not just interviews.
Coach slower communication under pressure: clarify, assign, confirm.
Build resilience through graduated responsibility before peak season.

evaluationScale.label: Reactive
evaluationScale.description: Escalates emotion, blame, or confusion when pressure rises.

evaluationScale.label: Unstable
evaluationScale.description: Performance and tone drop significantly under stress.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Handles routine pressure; struggles in ambiguous or high-stakes events.

evaluationScale.label: Composed
evaluationScale.description: Leads calmly, decides clearly, and stabilizes the team.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Elevates team performance when conditions are hardest.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Pressure does not build character—it reveals whether habits, preparation, and integrity hold.

pillars.name: Communication
pillars.tagline: The ability to convey expectations, listen actively, align teams, and drive clarity under operational complexity.
pillars.definition: Communication is turning plant priorities into shift-level clarity. It means direct expectations, active listening on the floor, respectful correction, and timely escalation with context.
pillars.whyItMatters: Most supervisor failures trace back to misalignment—not inability to run a machine. Missed handoffs, vague direction, and poor escalation create defects, downtime, and disengagement long before technical skill limits the leader.
behaviors: Sets clear expectations with outcomes, timing, and ownership
Confirms understanding before work begins—especially after changeovers
Delivers corrective feedback respectfully and specifically
Updates the team promptly when priorities or conditions shift
Escalates with facts, impact, and a recommended path forward
warningSigns: Assumes the team knows the plan without verification
Avoids difficult conversations or speaks in generalities
Messages differ by person, shift, or mood
Interrupts, dismisses, or fails to act on frontline input
Creates confusion during changeovers, launches, or crisis response
interviewQuestions: Tell me about a difficult message you delivered to your team.
How do you align priorities during a high-volume shift?
Describe a misunderstanding you caused and how you fixed it.
How do you communicate upward when your team is struggling?
coachingTips: Install a shift rhythm: start-up huddle, mid-shift check, handoff debrief.
Coach a simple structure: situation, expectation, impact, next step.
Require repeat-back on critical safety and quality instructions.
Evaluate communication on the floor during gemba—not in conference rooms.
Give feedback on clarity and tone, not just message content.

evaluationScale.label: Unclear
evaluationScale.description: Team lacks direction; issues repeat due to miscommunication.

evaluationScale.label: Inconsistent
evaluationScale.description: Message quality varies by situation or audience.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Adequate basics; improving listening and directness.

evaluationScale.label: Clear
evaluationScale.description: Aligns teams reliably and handles tough conversations well.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Creates exceptional clarity that accelerates execution and trust.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Clear communication multiplies every other leadership skill on the floor.

pillars.name: Team Impact
pillars.tagline: The ability to elevate the performance, accountability, and success of those around you.
pillars.definition: Team impact measures whether a leader makes the people around them better. Strong supervisors develop operators, strengthen culture, and leave the shift stronger than they found it.
pillars.whyItMatters: Production results scale through people. A supervisor who only personalizes output caps the team's potential. Leaders with team impact build bench strength, reduce turnover, and create shifts that perform with or without constant intervention.
behaviors: Coaches operators with feedback, follow-up, and opportunity
Shares credit openly when the shift succeeds
Improves measurable team metrics over time
Builds trust and mutual accountability across the crew
Develops relationships across shifts, maintenance, and quality
warningSigns: Story centers on personal heroics rather than team development
Rarely invests time in coaching or cross-training
Creates friction between shifts, departments, or roles
Takes credit for results the team earned
Cannot describe how others improved because of their leadership
interviewQuestions: Tell me about someone you helped succeed in a production role.
Describe a team you improved—what changed and how?
What would former operators say about working for you?
How do you address poor performance on your shift?
coachingTips: Judge supervisors by team trends: scrap, attendance, engagement, skill depth.
Set a development goal each quarter—every leader grows at least one person.
Observe crew behavior when the supervisor is absent; culture persists or fades.
Coach delegation and teaching, not doing the job for the team.
Track retention and internal promotions as signals of impact.

evaluationScale.label: Self-focused
evaluationScale.description: Personal output matters more than team capability or culture.

evaluationScale.label: Limited
evaluationScale.description: Minimal development; team performance plateaus.

evaluationScale.label: Developing
evaluationScale.description: Supports others reactively; coaching skills emerging.

evaluationScale.label: Multiplier
evaluationScale.description: Consistently elevates performance and develops individuals.

evaluationScale.label: Elite
evaluationScale.description: Builds future leaders; positive impact outlasts their assignment.

pillars.keyTakeaway: Leadership is measured by what the team becomes—not by what one person produces alone.
